cross.title: Osprey
cross.text: Ospreys that nest on Yellowstone's rivers and lakes fly south each autumn, and many winter on rivers in South America, including the Amazon basin. The same birds depend on fish in both places.
cross.when: Leaves Yellowstone in late summer and autumn and returns in spring.
cross.matters: Ospreys eat almost only fish, so they need clean, fish-rich water at both ends of the trip. Harm to either end hurts the same birds.

cross.title: Migratory shorebirds
cross.text: Shorebirds such as ruddy turnstones breed on Arctic tundra and winter on coasts as far south as Australia, including reef flats. Losing winter feeding grounds hurts the Arctic breeding population.
cross.when: Breed on the Arctic tundra in summer, then travel south for the northern winter.
cross.matters: Their long trip depends on a few feeding stops. Losing winter feeding grounds hurts the Arctic breeding population.

cross.title: Saharan dust
cross.text: Each year winds carry mineral dust, including phosphorus, from the Sahara across the Atlantic to the Amazon. It helps replace nutrients that heavy rain washes out of the soil.
cross.when: Strongest in winter and spring, when the winds carry the most dust across the Atlantic.
cross.matters: Heavy rain washes phosphorus out of rainforest soil. Dust from the Sahara helps replace part of what is lost.

cross.title: American white pelican
cross.text: American white pelicans nest on lakes across interior North America and winter on the Gulf coast. Wikipedia also says they follow the Mississippi River north as far as St. Paul in winter.
cross.when: Nest on inland lakes in spring and summer; spend the winter on the Gulf coast.
cross.matters: They need undisturbed nesting lakes in summer and fish-rich shallows in winter.

cross.title: River nutrients to the Gulf
cross.text: The Mississippi drains about 41% of the continental US. Its nitrogen and phosphorus, mostly from farm runoff and sewage, feed the algal blooms behind the Gulf's summer dead zone. Wikipedia, citing a NOAA fact sheet, attributes about 70% of the nutrient load to this basin.
cross.when: Flows all year; spring floods bring the biggest load, and the dead zone is largest in summer.
cross.matters: Too much nitrogen and phosphorus feeds algae. When the algae die and rot they use up oxygen near the sea floor, and fish and shellfish leave or die.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Gulf of Mexico dead zone

cross.title: Osprey (Chesapeake)
cross.text: Ospreys that breed around the Chesapeake Bay head south each autumn, and many winter in northern South America, including the Amazon basin. They return in spring to the same bay.
cross.when: Leave the bay in autumn and return in spring.
cross.matters: Ospreys need fish at the bay and on their winter rivers. Harm to either end hurts the same birds.

cross.title: Red knot
cross.text: Red knots refuel on the Wadden Sea mudflats and then fly on to winter on the coast of West Africa, including Banc d'Arguin in Mauritania. Both sites matter for the same birds.
cross.when: Stop on the Wadden Sea mudflats in spring and autumn, between the Arctic and West Africa.
cross.matters: Knots fatten up on a few rich mudflats. Losing one of them can leave birds too weak to finish the trip.

cross.title: Greater flamingo
cross.text: Greater flamingos ringed in the Camargue are regularly seen in Doñana and other western Mediterranean wetlands. The birds move between them as water levels change.
cross.when: Move between wetlands through the year as water levels rise and fall.
cross.matters: Flamingos depend on a network of shallow wetlands. If one dries out or is disturbed, birds move to another.

cross.title: Altiplano flamingos
cross.text: Chilean flamingos move between high-altitude lakes on the Andean plateau, from the salt lakes of southern Bolivia to Lake Titicaca. Shallow lakes dry up and fill with the seasons.
cross.when: Move with the seasons as shallow lakes fill and dry up.
cross.matters: Chilean flamingos feed in shallow salt lakes, so they need several lakes across the plateau.

cross.title: Western Arctic caribou
cross.text: The Western Arctic caribou herd migrates across northern Alaska and passes through both Kobuk Valley and Gates of the Arctic. Its river crossings in autumn are a major event at Kobuk.
cross.when: Move north in spring to calve and south again before winter; river crossings at Kobuk peak in autumn.
cross.matters: Caribou follow food across a huge area. Wolves, bears and people along the route depend on their passing.

cross.title: Pacific sockeye
cross.text: Sockeye salmon from Alaska's Bristol Bay rivers and from Kamchatka share the North Pacific while at sea. Each run then returns to its own river and feeds bears, eagles and forests.
cross.when: Spend a few years at sea, then adults return to their home rivers in summer to spawn.
cross.matters: Spawning salmon feed bears, eagles and the trees along the river. Without a run, the forest loses a source of nutrients.

cross.title: Green sea turtle (Florida Keys)
cross.text: Green turtles graze the seagrass of Biscayne Bay and nest and feed around the Dry Tortugas. They travel along the Florida reef tract between the two.
cross.when: Adults nest in summer and travel between feeding and nesting sites; hatchlings go to sea.
cross.matters: Turtles graze seagrass, which keeps it healthy. They need both safe nesting beaches and seagrass beds.

cross.title: Green sea turtle (Caribbean)
cross.text: Green turtles tagged in Florida have been tracked to feeding grounds across the Caribbean, where seagrass beds such as those in the Virgin Islands support them.
cross.when: Adults nest in summer and travel between feeding and nesting sites; hatchlings go to sea.
cross.matters: Turtles graze seagrass, which keeps it healthy. They need both safe nesting beaches and seagrass beds.

cross.title: Monarch butterfly
cross.text: Monarchs from the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada travel 1,200 to 2,800 miles or more to the mountain forests of central Mexico, including the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve. No single butterfly flies the whole round trip; it takes several generations.
cross.when: Monarchs head south in late summer and autumn, rest in Mexico from early November to mid-March, and their offspring come back north through spring and summer.
cross.matters: Milkweed is the monarch caterpillar's only host plant. Its loss and climate change have disturbed breeding and migration, and numbers have fallen over the past two decades.

cross.title: Great white pelican
cross.text: More than half of Eurasia's great white pelicans breed in the Danube Delta. Many western birds probably stop over in Israel on their autumn migration, as at the Hula Valley. The full routes are only partly known.
cross.when: They reach the Danube in late March or early April and leave after breeding, between September and late November.
cross.matters: The species is listed under the Convention on Migratory Species. Where European pelicans spend winter is not exactly known.

cross.title: Western marsh harrier
cross.text: Western marsh harriers breed across Europe, and most populations migrate. Many winter in the Sahel and the Nile basin, others in Arabia and the Indian subcontinent. Hortobágy in Hungary is a breeding wetland; Djoudj in Senegal is in the Sahel.
cross.when: Migratory birds spend winter in warmer regions and return to breed in Europe.
cross.matters: Marsh harriers are strongly tied to wetlands, especially those rich in reeds. Both ends of this trip are protected wetlands.

cross.title: Snow goose
cross.text: Snow geese nest north of the treeline. Greater snow geese fly the Atlantic Flyway to winter on the Atlantic coastal plain, around places like Delaware Bay. Spring flights can cover more than 3,000 miles back to the tundra.
cross.when: They nest from late May to mid-August and spend more than half the year travelling between nesting and wintering areas.
cross.matters: Geese have moved from coastal marsh to farm fields, and their numbers have grown. Too many geese now overgraze the tundra where they breed.

cross.title: Arctic fox
cross.text: In winter most Arctic foxes stay within their home range. A few, about 3 in 100, wander far, and some Canadian foxes travel from the Canadian archipelago to Greenland. Foxes living near coastal goose colonies are less likely to leave.
cross.when: Most foxes stay put in winter; the long trips are rare.
cross.matters: Foxes that make these long trips die at more than three times the rate of foxes that stay.
